hook.text: Why do the poor defend the rich? Why do workers vote against their interests? Gramsci called it hegemony.

buildup.text: Hegemony is domination through consent. The powerful shape culture so their rule seems natural and inevitable.

discovery.text: Antonio Gramsci argued that ruling classes maintain power by controlling ideas, education, media, and common sense.

twist.text: Hegemony is never complete. Counter-narratives, resistance, and alternative visions always challenge dominant ideas.

climax.text: Hegemony shows that the deepest power isn't physical. It's the power to define reality and make domination normal.

punchline.text: The strongest chains are the ones you can't see.

quiz.question: What is hegemony?
options: Domination through consent by making power seem natural

details.summary: Antonio Gramsci's concept of hegemony describes how dominant groups maintain power not just through force but by making their worldview seem natural and inevitable. When the oppressed accept ruling-class ideas as common sense, coercion becomes unnecessary.
details.whyItMatters: Hegemony explains why people often support systems that disadvantage them. Understanding how dominant ideologies become common sense reveals the mechanisms of invisible power that shape political consciousness.
takeaways: Hegemony maintains power by making domination seem natural
Ruling ideologies become common sense accepted by the dominated
Understanding hegemony reveals invisible mechanisms of power

faq.question: How does hegemony differ from coercion?
faq.answer: Coercion forces compliance through violence or threat. Hegemony achieves compliance through consent — people accept the dominant ideology as natural, inevitable, and beneficial. When workers believe the rich deserve their wealth because they worked harder, that is hegemony functioning successfully.

faq.question: Can hegemony be challenged?
faq.answer: Yes. Gramsci argued that counter-hegemonic movements create alternative worldviews that challenge dominant common sense. Education, media, art, and political organizing can expose the constructed nature of hegemonic ideas and propose alternatives. This is a constant cultural and political struggle.
